item.title: "Prediction" vs "Ground Truth": Where Do AI "Answers" Come From?
item.author: 0make@gmail.com (AZ)
item.description:
Introduction

The Most Intuitive Analogy: “Prediction” is the answer AI writes down in the exam hall, while “Ground Truth” is the standard answer key held by the teacher.

The essence of neural network training is to let AI continuously solve problems, then compare its “predictions” with “ground truth labels” to see how wrong it is (calculate Loss), and then adjust parameters (gradient descent).

However, depending on the AI’s learning mode (supervised learning vs reinforcement learning), the “sources” of these two things are very different. Let’s break it down in detail using the poker AI (Ding Ge Dan) you care about and everyday AI (such as cat recognition).

1. How Does Ground Truth (Label) Come About?

Ground truth is “the absolutely correct standard answer”. Its source depends on what game AI is playing:

1.1 In “Supervised Learning” (Such as Cat Recognition, Machine Translation)

Source: Human labor annotation or existing data pairs.

  • Cat Recognition: After human engineers collect 1 million cat images, they must manually label each image. For example, label one image as Label = 1 (representing cat), and label a dog image as Label = 0 (representing dog). These labels are hardcoded in the dataset files in advance.

  • Machine Translation: Chinese-English sentence pairs written by human translators. Input “你好”, the standard answer label is “Hello”.

1.2 In “Reinforcement Learning” (Such as DouZero Playing “Ding Ge Dan”, AlphaGo)

Source: Final settlement of the game environment or Monte Carlo simulation.

In poker AI, no human will label each move with a “standard answer” (because the situation is too complex for humans to label). Its “ground truth” is “played out” in the virtual environment.

Ground Truth (GGG) in DMC (Deep Monte Carlo):

After AI completes a full game of “Ding Ge Dan” at the virtual card table, the system determines win or loss according to the rules.

  • If AI wins this round, the environment returns a ground truth: G=+1G = +1G=+1
  • If AI loses this round, the environment returns: G=−1G = -1G=−1

This +1+1+1 or −1-1−1 is the “ground truth” shared by all steps in this game. It is derived from real execution through physical rules (game engine), without any subjective speculation.

2. How Does Prediction (Y^\hat{Y}Y^) Come About?

Prediction is the result that AI “guesses” after layer-by-layer calculation through its own brain (neural network) based on current input. Its generation process is Forward Propagation.

2.1 The Production Pipeline of Predictions

  1. Input Features (XXX): Convert current state into numbers. For example, encode “Ding Ge Dan” hand cards into a vector containing 300 numbers
  2. Network Calculation: These 300 numbers enter the neural network, passing through countless “matrix multiplication + activation functions” we discussed earlier, layer by layer
  3. Output Layer (Y^\hat{Y}Y^): Data reaches the last layer of the network (output layer), spitting out the final prediction

2.2 What Does Prediction Look Like? (Depends on Task Type)

In Classification Tasks (Such as Image Recognition):

The output layer usually connects with a Softmax activation function. It converts results into probabilities.

AI’s Prediction: [Cat probability: 0.85, Dog probability: 0.10, Bird probability: 0.05]

In Regression/Value Estimation Tasks (Such as Poker AI Predicting Win Rate):

The output layer is usually linear output (no activation function, or using Tanh), directly spitting out a specific numerical value.

AI’s Prediction: The network predicts that playing this card currently has a final win rate of Q=0.65Q = 0.65Q=0.65 (i.e., 65% confidence of winning).

3. When “Prediction” Meets “Ground Truth”: Calculating Loss (Error)

Now, AI has submitted its exam paper. The teacher (Loss Function) starts checking answers.

Scenario A: Cat Recognition (Classification Task)

  • Ground Truth: This image is clearly a cat, label is [1, 0, 0]
  • Prediction: AI guessed [0.85, 0.10, 0.05]
  • Calculate Loss (Cross-Entropy): The teacher found that AI guessed correctly, but not confidently enough (didn’t give 1.0), so calculated a smaller Loss value (such as 0.15). If AI guessed [0.1, 0.8, 0.1] (mistaking cat for dog), the Loss value would explode (such as becoming 2.5)

Scenario B: Playing “Ding Ge Dan” (Reinforcement Learning / DMC)

  • Ground Truth (GGG): This game is over, AI won, the environment gives the true outcome of +1+1+1
  • Prediction (QQQ): At step 10 of the game, AI’s neural network predicted its current situation’s win rate as 0.40.40.4
  • Calculate Loss (Mean Squared Error MSE):
Loss=(Prediction−GroundTruth)2=(0.4−1)2=(−0.6)2=0.36Loss = (Prediction - Ground Truth)^2 = (0.4 - 1)^2 = (-0.6)^2 = 0.36Loss=(Prediction−GroundTruth)2=(0.4−1)2=(−0.6)2=0.36

The teacher discovered: AI was too pessimistic at step 10 (only predicted 40% win rate), but actually won this round (100%). AI seriously underestimated its hand strength, producing an error of 0.36.

4. Summary: Their Position in the Training Loop

Now, we can completely map out the “data flow” of the entire deep learning training:

  1. Prepare Answers: Take out ground truth from the dataset (manually labeled cats, or +1+1+1 from poker environment settlement)
  2. AI Solves Problems: Feed input data (image pixels, or current hand cards) to the neural network, go through forward propagation, obtain predictions
  3. Teacher Grades: Use loss function to compare “predictions” and “ground truth”, calculate Loss (error)
  4. Backward Accountability: Through backpropagation (calculus chain rule), calculate gradients of Loss with respect to each weight
  5. Modify Brain: Through gradient descent, fine-tune the neural network’s weights

One-Sentence Summary: Ground truth is objective fact (given by humans, or calculated by rules), it never changes; prediction is AI’s subjective guess, it becomes closer and closer to ground truth as network weights are continuously adjusted (gradient descent). When predictions infinitely approach ground truth, we say: this model training has “converged”, and AI has graduated.

item.title: How Does Gradient Descent Actually Adjust Model Parameters? From Micro Operations to Macro Optimization
item.author: 0make@gmail.com (AZ)
item.description:
Introduction

To understand “how exactly” gradient descent adjusts model parameters, we need to zoom in from the macroscopic “blindfolded mountain descent” to the microscopic “mathematical operation” level.

Simply put, the essential action of gradient descent parameter adjustment is: “Based on the ‘accountability’ result (gradient) of each parameter’s contribution to the error, move the parameter slightly in the opposite direction that reduces the error.”

To help you see clearly this “fine-tuning” mechanical process, we break it down into three levels: from micro-level single parameter adjustment, to macro-level network-wide computation, and finally to advanced tuning techniques used in modern large models.

1. Micro Anatomy: The “Punishment” Process of a Single Weight

Suppose there is only one extremely simple weight parameter www in the neural network (such as the connection line between the “has bomb in hand” feature and “playing win rate”), and the current loss function (error) is LLL.

After forward propagation and backpropagation, we calculate the partial derivative (i.e., gradient) of loss LLL with respect to weight www: ∂L∂w\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}∂w∂L​.

1.1 What Does the Gradient Tell Us?

Suppose we calculate ∂L∂w=+2\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = +2∂w∂L​=+2.

This positive number +2 contains two key pieces of information:

  • Direction (positive sign): If www increases, error LLL will also increase
  • Magnitude (value 2): For every 1 unit increase in www, error LLL will increase by 2 units

1.2 How Are Parameters Adjusted?

Our ultimate goal is to make error LLL smaller. Since increasing www leads to increased LLL, we must decrease www.

At this point, Learning Rate (denoted as α\alphaα) comes into play. Suppose we set α=0.1\alpha = 0.1α=0.1 (meaning we only dare to fine-tune by 10% each time).

Update Formula Execution:

wnew=wold−α×∂L∂ww_{new} = w_{old} - \alpha \times \frac{\partial L}{\partial w}wnew​=wold​−α×∂w∂L​

Substituting specific numbers (assuming original wold=0.5w_{old} = 0.5wold​=0.5):

wnew=0.5−(0.1×2)=0.5−0.2=0.3w_{new} = 0.5 - (0.1 \times 2) = 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.3wnew​=0.5−(0.1×2)=0.5−0.2=0.3

Result: Weight www is adjusted from 0.5 to 0.3.

Significance: Because the model discovered that this weight was “counterproductive” (causing error to increase), it forcefully pulled it in the opposite direction. In the next forward propagation, this feature’s impact on the result becomes smaller, and the error decreases accordingly.

💡 Conversely: If the calculated gradient is -2, it means increasing www can reduce error, so the minus sign in the formula becomes a plus sign, increasing www.

2. Macro Perspective: The “Great Migration” of Millions of Parameters

In real neural networks (such as poker AI or Transformer), there aren’t just 1 parameter, but millions or even billions. How does gradient descent adjust them all simultaneously?

2.1 Not Loops, But “Matrix Parallelism”

In code (such as PyTorch), we absolutely do not write a for loop to update parameters one by one—that would be too slow.

  • All weights are organized into huge Tensors (multi-dimensional matrices)
  • The gradients calculated by backpropagation are also gradient tensors with exactly the same shape as the weights
  • The parameter update operation is executed at the bottom layer by GPU performing large-scale matrix subtraction

2.2 The Real Face at Code Level

If you open the source code of deep learning frameworks, the core logic of parameter adjustment (taking SGD as an example) in the underlying C++/CUDA code looks roughly like this:

# Pseudocode: Parallel parameter update on GPU
# params: list of tensors containing all weights and biases
# grads: list of corresponding gradient tensors calculated by backpropagation

for param, grad in zip(params, grads):
 # Core action: parameter = parameter - learning_rate * gradient
 # This step performs parallel subtraction on millions of floating-point numbers simultaneously on GPU
 param.data.sub_(learning_rate * grad.data) 
 
 # Optional: if there is weight decay (regularization), also subtract a portion of the parameter itself
 # param.data.sub_(weight_decay * param.data)

This is the physical truth of “how exactly adjustment happens”: in each training iteration (Step), the GPU multiplies millions of gradient matrices by the learning rate, then forcibly subtracts (or adds) these values from the original weight matrices. The network structure doesn’t change, but the “blood (weight values)” flowing inside is completely replaced once.

3. Modern Advanced: The “Senior Tuners” Behind Large Models

If you only understand the basic formula above (called SGD, Stochastic Gradient Descent), you only understand deep learning before 2015.

When training ChatGPT (Transformer LLM) or Stable Diffusion, pure SGD faces two fatal problems:

  1. Easy to get stuck in local minima: Reaching a small pit halfway up the mountain where gradient is 0, then stopping there
  2. Difficult to unify learning rate: Some parameters need big fast steps, others need small slow steps; a globally unified learning rate α\alphaα performs poorly

Therefore, how does modern AI actually tune parameters? The answer is using advanced optimizers, the most famous being Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation).

Adam makes two extremely clever “modifications” to basic gradient descent:

3.1 Modification 1: Introducing “Momentum” — Descending Like Pushing a Snowball

Principle: Adam not only looks at the current gradient but also records the gradient directions from previous steps.

  • If gradients point in the same direction for several consecutive steps, it gives the parameter an “inertia” (acceleration)
  • If gradient directions oscillate back and forth, it cancels out this oscillation

Effect: Makes parameters “slide” faster on smooth error surfaces and less likely to get stuck in small pits.

3.2 Modification 2: Adaptive Learning Rate — Giving Each Parameter Different “Shoes”

Principle: Adam records the sum of squared historical gradients for each parameter.

  • If a parameter (such as rare word embeddings) is rarely updated, having small squared gradient sum, Adam automatically increases its learning rate, letting it learn faster
  • If a parameter (such as common words like “the”, “is”) is updated extremely frequently, having large squared gradient sum, Adam automatically decreases its learning rate, preventing it from “over-learning” and destroying existing knowledge

Effect: Achieves “personalized” parameter adjustment for each parameter, greatly accelerating convergence.

4. Summary: The Complete Lifecycle of Parameter Adjustment

Now, we can string together the complete process of “gradient descent adjusting parameters”:

4.1 Perceiving Error

AI makes predictions and calculates the gap (Loss) between predicted values and true outcomes (such as poker wins/losses).

4.2 Backward Accountability

Using calculus chain rule, calculate backwards from the output layer to precisely determine the partial derivatives (gradients) of Loss with respect to every weight in the network. This is equivalent to issuing a “penalty ticket” to each parameter, telling it: “Here’s how much you caused the error to increase/decrease this time; the responsibility is yours.”

4.3 Advanced Decision-Making

Optimizers like Adam receive these “penalty tickets” and, combining historical memory (momentum) and update frequency (adaptive), calculate the actual step size and direction each parameter should truly move.

4.4 Physical Execution

GPU activates, performing parallel matrix subtraction between millions of weight matrices and the calculated adjustment amounts.

4.5 Rebirth

Old weights are overwritten, new weights are born. The neural network completes a tiny “evolution”.

Core Insight: After tens of millions of such “perceive → accountability → decision → execute” cycles, those originally randomly generated numbers are gradually sculpted by the invisible chisel of gradient descent into “artificial intelligence” capable of understanding language, winning at poker, and even generating stunningly beautiful images.

item.title: Self-Attention Mechanism Intuitively Explained
item.author: 0make@gmail.com (AZ)
item.description:
Introduction

One-sentence summary: Self-Attention mechanism allows every element in a sequence (such as each word in a sentence) to “rate” all other elements in the sequence, and then decides who to “focus on” when understanding itself based on the scores.

Self-Attention is the soul of the Transformer architecture and the key that enables modern Large Language Models (LLMs) to understand context. We can temporarily set aside complex mathematics and first feel it through an intuitive life scenario, then break down its core logic and formulas.

This article will take you from the “social circle” of words, through the perfect analogy of library book searching, and finally into the mathematical essence of Q, K, V, allowing you to thoroughly understand this core technology that changed the AI landscape.

1. The Most Intuitive Analogy: The “Social Circle” of Words

Suppose we have this sentence:

“Apple” company released new “Apple” phone.

In traditional Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), AI reads words one by one from left to right. When it reaches the second “Apple”, it may have somewhat forgotten the previous context.

But in Self-Attention mechanism, AI sees the entire sentence at once. When processing the second “Apple”, it sends signals to all words in the sentence for “relevance scoring”:

Word Seen Score Reason
“company” +0.8 Because companies can own Apple
“released” +0.9 Because the subject of the release action is company/Apple
“phone” +0.95 Because phone directly modifies Apple, determining that this “Apple” is a tech product, not a fruit
“new”, “.” +0.1 Because they are function words with low information content

Result: When updating its internal representation, the second “Apple” absorbs features from “phone”, “released”, and “company” in large amounts, thereby accurately understanding its meaning here. This is “attention” - allocating limited computational resources to the most relevant words.

This mechanism solves two fatal flaws of traditional RNN:

  1. Long-range dependency problem: No matter how far apart two words are, they can establish direct connections
  2. Parallel computation advantage: No need to process sequentially, can compute attention weights for all words simultaneously

2. The Core Trio: Query (Q), Key (K), Value (V)

The reason Self-Attention can achieve the above process relies on three extremely clever vectors (can be understood as three different “feature extractors”): Q, K, V.

We can perfectly metaphor them using “Library Book Searching”:

  • Query (Q, query vector): Represents “Who am I now, what am I looking for”. Like the “borrowing request form” in your hand.
  • Key (K, key vector): Represents “What features do I have, what can I provide”. Like the “labels/indexes” on each book spine in the library.
  • Value (V, value vector): Represents “My actual content/essence”. Like the “specific content” after opening the book.

Workflow

When word A in the sentence wants to update its understanding:

  1. Word A takes out its Q (need)
  2. Word A uses this Q to match and calculate (usually dot product) with K (labels) of all words in the sentence (including itself). Higher match means higher score
  3. Convert these scores into probability weights (sum to 1) through Softmax function
  4. Finally, use these weights to perform weighted summation on V (actual content) of all words

Result: Word A obtains a new “super representation” that integrates the essence of the entire sentence.

Why Three Vectors?

You might ask: Why not directly use the word’s own vector, but separately generate Q, K, V?

The answer lies in flexibility:

  • The same word may need to play different roles in different contexts
  • Q focuses on “what I want to know”
  • K focuses on “what information I can provide”
  • V focuses on “what my substantive content is”

By linearly transforming the original word vector into three different spaces, the model can learn richer semantic relationships.

3. The Core Trio: Query (Q), Key (K), Value (V)

The reason Self-Attention can achieve the above process relies on three extremely clever vectors (can be understood as three different “feature extractors”): Q, K, V.

We can perfectly metaphor them using “Library Book Searching”:

  • Query (Q, query vector): Represents “Who am I now, what am I looking for”. Like the “borrowing request form” in your hand.
  • Key (K, key vector): Represents “What features do I have, what can I provide”. Like the “labels/indexes” on each book spine in the library.
  • Value (V, value vector): Represents “My actual content/essence”. Like the “specific content” after opening the book.

How Are Q, K, V Generated?

Q, K, V are not manually set, nor are they fixed. They are dynamically calculated from each word’s “initial word embedding” through “matrix multiplication” during the model’s training process.

In other words, Q, K, V are “learned” by the model itself.

To help you thoroughly understand this process, let’s break down how this “magic” happens in four steps.

Step 1: Starting Point — The Word’s “Initial ID Card” (Word Embedding)

When a sentence (such as “Apple released phone”) is input to Transformer, the model first converts each word into a fixed-length string of numbers, called Word Embedding.

For example, “Apple” might be represented as a 512-dimensional vector: [0.2, -0.5, 0.8, ..., 0.1].

This initial vector contains the basic meaning of the word in the dictionary, but it is not yet Q, K, or V. We call the matrix containing all word vectors XXX.

Step 2: Core Magic — Three Different “Filters” (Weight Matrices)

Inside the Transformer model, there are three learnable weight matrices, which we call WQW_QWQ​, WKW_KWK​, and WVW_VWV​.

When the model first starts training, the numbers in these three matrices are completely random.

As the model trains through massive amounts of text using “gradient descent”, the numbers in these three matrices are continuously fine-tuned, eventually learning how to extract the most useful information.

You can think of these three matrices as three different “filters” or “questioners”:

  • WQW_QWQ​ (Query filter): Specifically used to extract “what information does this word currently need”
  • WKW_KWK​ (Key filter): Specifically used to extract “what feature labels can this word provide”
  • WVW_VWV​ (Value filter): Specifically used to extract “the actual semantic content of this word”

Step 3: Calculation Process — Simple Matrix Multiplication

The process of determining Q, K, V is mathematically extremely simple—just a matrix multiplication:

Q=X⋅WQQ = X \cdot W_QQ=X⋅WQ​K=X⋅WKK = X \cdot W_KK=X⋅WK​V=X⋅WVV = X \cdot W_VV=X⋅WV​

How exactly is it calculated?

Suppose “Apple”’s initial word vector xapplex_{apple}xapple​ is a 512-dimensional vector, and WQW_QWQ​ is a 512×64512 \times 64512×64 matrix.

When xapplex_{apple}xapple​ is multiplied by WQW_QWQ​, the 512-dimensional initial information is “compressed” and “reorganized” into a new 64-dimensional vector, which is qappleq_{apple}qapple​ for “Apple” in this specific context.

Similarly, using the same xapplex_{apple}xapple​ to multiply with WKW_KWK​ and WVW_VWV​ yields kapplek_{apple}kapple​ and vapplev_{apple}vapple​.

💡 Key point: The same word (same initial vector XXX), because it’s multiplied by different weight matrices (WQ,WK,WVW_Q, W_K, W_VWQ​,WK​,WV​), splits into three different vectors (Q, K, V), each undertaking different tasks.

Step 4: Intuitive Analogy: The Job Seeker’s “Triple Identity”

To better understand, let’s imagine each word as a job seeker (initial word vector XXX), and WQ,WK,WVW_Q, W_K, W_VWQ​,WK​,WV​ as three different evaluation forms set up by the HR department:

  1. Calculating Q (Query): HR gives the job seeker a form: “What kind of team collaboration are you currently most eager to find?” After filling it out, the job seeker gets his Q (need).
  2. Calculating K (Key): HR gives the job seeker another form: “Please list your top 3 core skill tags.” After filling it out, the job seeker gets his K (label).
  3. Calculating V (Value): HR gives the job seeker a third form: “Please describe in detail your past actual project experience and capabilities.” After filling it out, the job seeker gets his V (substantive content).

After all job seekers (all words in the sentence) complete these three forms, the self-attention mechanism begins to operate:

“Apple” takes its Q (need) and matches/scores against the K (labels) of “released” and “phone”. Finding an extremely high match with “phone”’s K, “Apple” then absorbs a large amount of “phone”’s V (substantive content), updating its understanding of the current context.

Workflow Summary

When word A in the sentence wants to update its understanding:

  1. Word A takes out its Q (need)
  2. Word A uses this Q to match and calculate (usually dot product) with K (labels) of all words in the sentence (including itself). Higher match means higher score
  3. Convert these scores into probability weights (sum to 1) through Softmax function
  4. Finally, use these weights to perform weighted summation on V (actual content) of all words

Result: Word A obtains a new “super representation” that integrates the essence of the entire sentence.

Why Three Vectors?

You might ask: Why not directly use the word’s own vector, but separately generate Q, K, V?

The answer lies in flexibility:

  • The same word may need to play different roles in different contexts
  • Q focuses on “what I want to know”
  • K focuses on “what information I can provide”
  • V focuses on “what my substantive content is”

By linearly transforming the original word vector into three different spaces, the model can learn richer semantic relationships.

4. Multi-Head Attention

In actual Transformers, usually not just one set of Q, K, V is used, but multiple sets (called “heads”).

Why Multi-Head?

You might ask: Is one set of WQ,WK,WVW_Q, W_K, W_VWQ​,WK​,WV​ enough?

The answer is: No. Because a word often has multiple meanings in a sentence.

This is why Transformer introduces “Multi-Head Attention”.

The model doesn’t just learn one set of WQ,WK,WVW_Q, W_K, W_VWQ​,WK​,WV​, but learns 8 sets, 12 sets, or even more (called 8 “heads”).

  • Head 1’s weight matrix might learn to focus on grammatical relationships (e.g., “Apple”’s Q matches “released”’s K to determine subject-verb relationship)
  • Head 2’s weight matrix might learn to focus on semantic modification (e.g., “Apple”’s Q matches “phone”’s K to determine it’s a tech product)
  • Head 3’s weight matrix might learn to focus on reference relationships (e.g., the second “it”’s Q matches the first “Apple”’s K)

Imagine:

  • Head 1 might focus on grammatical relationships (subject-verb-object structure)
  • Head 2 might focus on semantic relationships (synonyms, antonyms)
  • Head 3 might focus on reference relationships (which noun does the pronoun refer to)
  • Head 4 might focus on sentiment orientation (positive, negative)

Each head understands the sentence from different perspectives, and finally concatenates the outputs of all heads to form a more comprehensive representation.

Multi-Head Attention Calculation Process

  1. Project Q, K, V into hhh different subspaces respectively
  2. Independently calculate attention in each subspace
  3. Concatenate outputs of all heads
  4. Then pass through a linear transformation to get the final output
MultiHead(Q,K,V)=Concat(head1,...,headh)WO\text{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, ..., \text{head}_h)W^OMultiHead(Q,K,V)=Concat(head1​,...,headh​)WO

Where each head:

headi=Attention(QWiQ,KWiK,VWiV)\text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V)headi​=Attention(QWiQ​,KWiK​,VWiV​)

Finally, the model concatenates the results calculated by these 8 heads, then undergoes another linear transformation to obtain the word’s final, extremely rich contextual representation.

5. Intuitive Breakdown of the Formula

The core formula of Self-Attention is very elegant and is the soul of the entire Transformer:

Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKTdk)V\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)VAttention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QKT​)V

Let’s break it down into four steps (assuming we’re processing a sentence, Q, K, V are all matrices, each row represents a word):

Step 1: Calculate Relevance Scores (QKTQK^TQKT)

QQQ multiplied by the transpose of KKK (KTK^TKT), mathematically means calculating the dot product (inner product) of QQQ with each KKK.

Physical meaning: The larger the dot product, the more consistent the directions of the two vectors, meaning the “query need” and “feature label” match better, resulting in higher relevance scores.

For example:

  • If Q points in the “tech product” direction and K also points in the “tech product” direction, the dot product will be large
  • If Q points in the “fruit” direction while K points in the “tech product” direction, the dot product will be small or even negative

Step 2: Scaling (÷dk\div \sqrt{d_k}÷dk​​)

dkd_kdk​ is the vector dimension. Dividing by dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ prevents dot product results from becoming too large.

Physical meaning: If values are too large, the next Softmax function will extreme probabilities (become 1 and 0), causing gradient vanishing and making the model unable to learn. This is an engineering “stabilizer”.

Example:

  • Assume vector dimension dk=64d_k = 64dk​=64
  • Without scaling, dot products might range from [-100, 100]
  • After dividing by 64=8\sqrt{64} = 864​=8, the range becomes [-12.5, 12.5]
  • This makes Softmax output smoother, beneficial for gradient propagation

Step 3: Normalize Weights (softmax\text{softmax}softmax)

Convert all scores obtained in the previous step into a probability distribution summing to 1 through the Softmax function.

softmax(xi)=exi∑jexj\text{softmax}(x_i) = \frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}}softmax(xi​)=∑j​exj​exi​​

Physical meaning: Transform raw “matching scores” into “attention weights”. For example: 60% attention to “phone”, 30% to “released”, 10% to other words.

Softmax characteristics:

  • Sum of all output values is 1
  • Larger input values are amplified, smaller ones are compressed
  • Ensures interpretability of weights (probability distribution)

Step 4: Weighted Summation (×V\times V×V)

Use the weights calculated in step 3 to multiply with each word’s corresponding VVV (actual content), then sum them all up.

Physical meaning: This is the final “fusion” process. The current word absorbs information from the entire sentence, but the absorption ratio is entirely determined by attention weights.

Mathematical expression:

Outputi=∑jweightij⋅Vj\text{Output}_i = \sum_j \text{weight}_{ij} \cdot V_jOutputi​=j∑​weightij​⋅Vj​

Where weightij\text{weight}_{ij}weightij​ is the attention weight of word iii to word jjj.

6. Multi-Head Attention

In actual Transformers, usually not just one set of Q, K, V is used, but multiple sets (called “heads”).

Why Multi-Head?

Imagine:

  • Head 1 might focus on grammatical relationships (subject-verb-object structure)
  • Head 2 might focus on semantic relationships (synonyms, antonyms)
  • Head 3 might focus on reference relationships (which noun does the pronoun refer to)
  • Head 4 might focus on sentiment orientation (positive, negative)

Each head understands the sentence from different perspectives, and finally concatenates the outputs of all heads to form a more comprehensive representation.

Multi-Head Attention Calculation Process

  1. Project Q, K, V into hhh different subspaces respectively
  2. Independently calculate attention in each subspace
  3. Concatenate outputs of all heads
  4. Then pass through a linear transformation to get the final output
MultiHead(Q,K,V)=Concat(head1,...,headh)WO\text{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, ..., \text{head}_h)W^OMultiHead(Q,K,V)=Concat(head1​,...,headh​)WO

Where each head:

headi=Attention(QWiQ,KWiK,VWiV)\text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V)headi​=Attention(QWiQ​,KWiK​,VWiV​)

7. Why Called “Self” Attention?

In early machine translation models (such as Seq2Seq + Attention), the attention mechanism was cross-sequence: for example, using Q from Chinese sentences to match K from English sentences, called “Cross-Attention”.

The brilliance of Self-Attention lies in: Q, K, V all come from the same sequence (the same sentence) itself.

It doesn’t need external target sequences, but allows elements within the sentence to engage in “self-reflection” and “mutual communication”. Through this dense internal interaction, the model can directly establish connections between any two words (no matter how far apart they are in the sentence) in just one layer of computation.

Self-Attention vs Cross-Attention

Feature Self-Attention Cross-Attention
Q, K, V Source Same sequence Different sequences
Application Scenario Inside encoder, inside decoder Connection between decoder and encoder
Function Understand intra-sequence relationships Establish connections between source and target sequences
Example Understand the meaning of “Apple” in the sentence Translate Chinese “苹果” to English “apple”

8. Positional Encoding

Self-Attention has an inherent flaw: it doesn’t care about word order.

Because it sees the “entire sentence at once”, “I love you” and “You love me” might look the same to pure Self-Attention (just different weight distributions).

To solve this problem, Transformer introduces Positional Encoding, adding position information in the sentence to each word:

PE(pos,2i)=sin⁡(pos100002i/dmodel)PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right)PE(pos,2i)​=sin(100002i/dmodel​pos​)PE(pos,2i+1)=cos⁡(pos100002i/dmodel)PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right)PE(pos,2i+1)​=cos(100002i/dmodel​pos​)

Where:

  • pospospos is the word’s position in the sentence
  • iii is the dimension index
  • dmodeld_{model}dmodel​ is the model dimension

Thus, even if two words have the same content, as long as their positions differ, their final representations will be different.

9. Practical Applications: Potential of Self-Attention in “Ding Ge Dan” Project

Although “Ding Ge Dan” currently mainly uses DMC + DNN architecture, Self-Attention mechanism also has application value in certain scenarios:

9.1 Modeling Play History

In poker games, play history is sequential data. Using Self-Attention can:

  • Capture long-term dependency relationships (such as playing strategies from 10 rounds ago)
  • Identify opponent’s playing patterns
  • Simultaneously focus on multiple key historical nodes

9.2 Deep Understanding of Hand Features

Treating hands as a sequence (each card is an element), Self-Attention can:

  • Discover combination relationships between cards
  • Automatically learn which card types are more important
  • Be more flexible than manually designed features

9.3 Integration with LLM

As mentioned in our Transformer LLM vs Poker AI Technology Path Comparison:

  • DMC/DNN handles precise probability calculation and playing decisions
  • LLM (based on Self-Attention) handles opponent modeling, tactical analysis, and macro strategy

The two can work synergistically to form a stronger AI system.

10. Summary

The revolutionary aspects of Self-Attention mechanism:

  1. Global vision: No longer limited to local windows or sequential processing
  2. Dynamic weights: Dynamically adjust focus based on context
  3. Parallel computation: Fully utilize modern GPU parallel capabilities
  4. Interpretability: Attention weights can be visualized, helping us understand the model’s decision-making process

Core idea: Not all information is equally important; learning to “focus” is the key to intelligence.

From the “social circle” of words to the Q/K/V model of libraries, and then to elegant mathematical formulas, Self-Attention mechanism solves the core challenges of sequence modeling in a concise yet powerful way. This is why it became the cornerstone of Transformer architecture and ultimately gave birth to world-changing large language models like GPT and BERT.

item.title: Transformer LLM vs Poker AI: Two Different Tech Trees in Deep Learning
item.author: 0make@gmail.com (AZ)
item.description:
They are both products of Deep Learning, relying on the same underlying principles we discussed earlier—Deep Neural Networks (DNN), gradient descent—and ultimately saving weight parameter files. However, their brain structures (architectures), learning methods (training paradigms), and specialized tasks (objectives) are worlds apart.

We can summarize their differences in one sentence:

  • Transformer LLM (like ChatGPT, Qwen) is a “well-read scholar,” excelling at understanding context and generating coherent text.
  • Poker AI (like DouZero/DMC) is a “battle-hardened gambler,” skilled at calculating probabilities and making cold, profit-maximizing decisions under incomplete information.

Let’s dive into what Transformer LLM is and explore its core differences from Poker AI.

I. What Are Transformer and LLM?

1. Transformer: A Revolutionary “Network Architecture”

Before Transformer emerged (before 2017), sequence data (such as text and speech) was mainly processed using RNNs (Recurrent Neural Networks). Their drawback was “poor memory”—by the time they reached the end of a sentence, they often forgot the beginning.

In 2017, Google proposed the Transformer architecture, with its core innovation being the “Self-Attention Mechanism.”

Intuitive Understanding: When Transformer reads a sentence (for example: “In Dinggedan, multiple 4s can be used to swap cards played by the previous player”), it doesn’t read word by word from left to right. Instead, it sees the entire sentence at once and calculates the “relevance” between each word and all other words. When it encounters “swap,” the attention mechanism immediately assigns high weights to “4” and “previous player” mentioned earlier, instantly understanding the logical relationship between them.

Advantages: Extremely good at capturing long-distance dependencies and highly parallelizable, making it possible to train ultra-large models.

2. LLM (Large Language Model)

LLM is a super neural network built on the Transformer architecture and trained on massive amounts of text data (books, webpages, and code from the entire internet).

Its core task: Next-token Prediction. Given the first half of a sentence, it predicts the second half. Through trillions of such “fill-in-the-blank” training exercises, it implicitly learns grammar, logic, common sense, and even reasoning abilities.

II. Transformer LLM vs. Poker AI (DouZero/DMC)

Although both are called “AI,” if you want to develop a “Dinggedan” AI, directly using an existing LLM won’t work. Here’s a detailed comparison of their core differences:

Comparison Dimension Transformer LLM (e.g., Qwen, GPT) Poker AI (e.g., DouZero / DMC)
Core Architecture Transformer (relies on Self-Attention mechanism, processes variable-length sequences) MLP / CNN (Multi-Layer Perceptron or lightweight convolution, processes fixed-length feature vector matrices)
Learning Method Self-supervised learning (next-token prediction) + Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) + Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) Pure Reinforcement Learning, through massive self-play and Monte Carlo simulation (DMC)
Input Data Text sequences (Tokens), e.g., “I have two 4s, the previous player played a straight, what should I do?” Structured state vectors (State Vector), e.g., hand card encoding matrix, played card history, remaining cards
Output Result Probability distribution over vocabulary, used to generate the next word or a paragraph Value scores (Q-value) or play probabilities for each legal action
Error Tolerance Relatively high. Allows some degree of “hallucination” or nonsense as long as overall coherence is maintained Extremely low. Must strictly follow game rules (illegal actions are forcibly masked via Action Masking); one wrong move can cause the entire game to collapse
Ultimate Goal Generate text that best conforms to human language habits and logic Make decisions with the highest long-term expected win rate (win the game)

III. Why Can’t We Directly Use LLM to Play “Dinggedan”?

If you directly feed “Dinggedan” rules to a regular LLM and ask it to help you play cards, it will perform like an “armchair strategist who talks big but delivers little.” Here’s why:

1. Lack of Precise Probability Calculation Ability

LLMs are essentially “word chain masters.” They are not good at rigorous mathematical probability deduction. In poker endgames, where precise calculation of the opponent’s bomb probability is required, LLMs easily produce “hallucinations,” giving seemingly reasonable but actually losing suggestions.

2. Mismatched Action Space

LLM outputs are words, while poker’s legal actions change dynamically (for example, this round you can play a straight, next round only single cards). Making an LLM accurately output a poker action that complies with current rules from tens of thousands of words each time is extremely inefficient and prone to violations.

3. Different Training Objectives

The LLM’s training objective is “to make text look like it was written by humans,” not “to win this game.” It hasn’t undergone the brutal reinforcement learning baptism of tens of millions of rounds where “losing deducts points and winning adds points.”

IV. Frontier Trends: Can They Be Combined?

Although pure LLMs are not suitable for directly playing poker, in 2026’s cutting-edge AI research, the two are experiencing fascinating integration:

1. LLM as the “Cerebral Cortex” of Poker AI (High-Level Strategy Planning)

Traditional poker AI trained with DMC handles the底层 “precise calculation and card playing” (cerebellum), while LLM handles “opponent modeling and macro strategy” (cerebrum). For example, LLM analyzes the opponent’s playing habits from the past 10 games and summarizes in natural language: “The opponent is an aggressive player who likes to bluff with fake bombs.” This conclusion is then converted into feature vectors and input to the DMC network to guide exploitative decision-making.

2. Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning for LLM (RL for LLM)

Current research is attempting to let LLMs directly play text adventure games or simplified versions of poker. By using “game victory or defeat” as reward signals and applying reinforcement learning algorithms like PPO to fine-tune LLM weights, researchers force them to evolve from “speaking beautifully” to “winning.”

V. Conclusion

The core formula of Transformer LLM is:

Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKTdk)V\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)VAttention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QKT​)V

It performs pattern matching and sequence generation.

The core formula of Poker AI (DMC) is:

Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+α(G−Q(s,a))Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha(G - Q(s,a))Q(s,a)←Q(s,a)+α(G−Q(s,a))

It performs Markov decision-making and expected value maximization.

Both are great achievements of deep learning, just branched onto different “technology trees.” If you want to develop a “Dinggedan” AI, DouZero (DMC) remains the most reliable and efficient foundation; while Transformer LLM is better suited as the AI’s “commentator” or “senior tactical analyst.”

item.title: What Exactly Is a Trained Model File? Demystifying AI's "Brain Memory Backup"
item.author: 0make@gmail.com (AZ)
item.description:
Introduction

If you’ve ever trained a deep learning model, you’ve definitely encountered files with extensions like .pth, .h5, or .onnx. They might be only tens of megabytes or several gigabytes in size. But have you ever wondered: what exactly is inside these files?

If we compare a well-trained AI to a “master martial artist,” then this saved file is the “backup of the master’s brain memory.” It doesn’t contain any game graphics, rule code, or human card records—only pure mathematical parameters.

This article will take you through a detailed breakdown of model file components and use “Dinggedan AI” as an example to help you thoroughly understand the essence of modern AI.

I. What’s Inside the File? (Four Core Elements)

When you save a deep learning model, it typically packages the following four components:

1. Model Weights and Biases — The Core Soul

These are millions, tens of millions, or even billions of floating-point numbers (Float32 or Float16) that the neural network continuously fine-tunes during “gradient descent.”

In poker AI: These numerical matrices solidify the AI’s “card sense.” For instance, a specific combination of weight matrices represents the tactical intuition of “when holding two 4s and the previous player plays a straight, decisively swap cards.”

These weights are not randomly generated but are optimal solutions gradually adjusted through thousands of self-play games under the guidance of loss functions. Each number carries the AI’s judgment capability for specific situations.

2. Network Architecture / Computation Graph

This records how the weights are connected: how many layers there are, how many neurons per layer, and what activation functions are used (such as ReLU).

Note: Some frameworks (like PyTorch) only save weights, requiring you to redefine the network structure in code when loading; while others (like TensorFlow SavedModel) bundle both structure and weights together.

The network architecture is like the “skeleton” of the nervous system, determining how information flows between layers. Without this structure, weights would just be a bunch of meaningless numbers.

3. Optimizer State — For “Resume Training”

This records the state at training interruption (such as first and second moment estimates in the Adam optimizer).

If power suddenly fails after 3 days of training, with this file, you can continue training from the exact step where it stopped, without starting from scratch.

This is crucial for large model training. Imagine if your AI has already learned from 10 million poker games and the server suddenly crashes—without the optimizer state, you’d have to start over, meaning all previous computational resources would be wasted.

4. Metadata and Configuration

This records hyperparameters during training (such as learning rate α, number of epochs trained), vocabulary (for NLP models), or current training steps.

While this information doesn’t directly participate in inference, it’s very important for reproducing experimental results, continuing training, or debugging the model.

II. Common File Formats in Mainstream Frameworks

Depending on the deep learning framework you use, the file extensions and formats differ:

1. PyTorch (Currently the absolute mainstream in academia and poker AI like DouZero)

  • .pt or .pth: The most common extensions. Essentially a compressed Python Dictionary storing the aforementioned weights and tensors using key-value pairs.

  • .safetensors: A popular new format in recent years. Safer than .pth (won’t execute malicious code during loading) and loads extremely fast. Currently strongly recommended by communities like Hugging Face.

DouZero Example: After training completion, files like douzero_checkpoint.pth are typically generated.

2. TensorFlow / Keras

  • .h5 or .keras: HDF5 format single files containing model structure, weights, and training configuration, very convenient for portability.

  • SavedModel (Folder): TensorFlow’s official standard format. It’s a folder containing saved_model.pb (computation graph structure) and a variables/ subfolder (storing specific weight data).

3. Cross-Platform Deployment Formats (For deploying AI to mobile phones or web browsers)

  • .onnx (Open Neural Network Exchange): An open format led by Microsoft. You can convert PyTorch-trained .pth models to .onnx, then run them efficiently in C++, Java, or even browsers (ONNX.js) without installing the bulky PyTorch library.

  • .engine / .trt: NVIDIA TensorRT format, specifically optimized for extreme inference acceleration on NVIDIA GPUs.

III. Concrete Example: “Dinggedan AI”

Suppose you spent a week training a “Dinggedan” DMC model on a server and saved it as dinggedan_final.pth (possibly only tens of MB in size).

If you open it with Python code, you’ll see a structure like this:

python
import torch

# Load model file
checkpoint = torch.load('dinggedan_final.pth')

# View file contents
print(checkpoint.keys())
# Output might look like:
# dict_keys(['model_state_dict', 'optimizer_state_dict', 'epoch', 'loss'])

# View weight parameters
model_weights = checkpoint['model_state_dict']
for key, value in model_weights.items():
 print(f"{key}: shape={value.shape}, dtype={value.dtype}")
 
# For example:
# layer1.weight: shape=(128, 64), dtype=torch.float32
# layer1.bias: shape=(128,), dtype=torch.float32
# ...

item.title: Deep Monte-Carlo Algorithm (DMC): From Self-Play to Intuitive Decision-Making
item.author: 0make@gmail.com (AZ)
item.description:
Introduction

In the field of artificial intelligence, game playing has always been one of the most challenging problems. From Go to poker, different types of games impose vastly different requirements on algorithms. Today, we will delve into the Deep Monte-Carlo Algorithm (DMC), an innovative method that has demonstrated remarkable power in imperfect information games.

To summarize the principle of DMC in the simplest terms: Instead of relying on logical deduction to “imagine” the next move, it directly sees the “final outcome” through massive simulations, then uses deep neural networks to memorize and summarize “which action in which situation leads to the highest probability of winning.”

1. Core Components Breakdown

1.1 Monte Carlo (MC) Part: How to Evaluate Actions?

In reinforcement learning, there are traditionally two methods to evaluate the value Q(S,A)Q(S,A)Q(S,A) of an action AAA in state SSS:

Temporal Difference (TD, such as classic DQN)

Take one step, observe the immediate reward, and add an estimate of the “maximum value of the next step” (imagination). The formula is:

Target Value=Immediate Reward+γ×Maximum Predicted Value of Next Step\text{Target Value} = \text{Immediate Reward} + \gamma \times \text{Maximum Predicted Value of Next Step}Target Value=Immediate Reward+γ×Maximum Predicted Value of Next Step

This method relies on estimating future values, which can easily introduce bias.

Monte Carlo (MC)

Refuses imagination. It requires completing the entire game until a winner is determined. Then it backtracks and uses the final true total return (Return, denoted as GGG) of that game as the value label for every previous action.

Core characteristic of MC: It is unbiased. Because it uses the actual final outcome that occurred, without introducing any “erroneous estimates of the future.”

1.2 Deep (Deep Learning) Part: How to Remember Massive Situations?

Traditional Monte Carlo methods use a “lookup table” (Q-Table) to record the value of each state. However, in poker (or Ding Ge Dan), the number of states is astronomical (over 102010^{20}1020), making tables impossible to store.

Introduction of Deep Learning: DMC uses a Deep Neural Network (DNN) to replace the lookup table.

Role of the network: It acts as a “function approximator.” The input is the current situation features (hand cards, historical plays), and the output is the predicted win rate for each legal action.

2. Standard Execution Flow of DMC Algorithm

The training of DMC is a closed loop of “Self-Play → Collect Outcomes → Supervised Learning.” The specific steps are as follows:

2.1 Self-Play Sampling

Let the current neural network play against itself (or multiple instances). At each step, the network predicts the values of various actions based on the current situation StS_tSt​, and selects an action AtA_tAt​ to execute with some randomness, continuing until the game ends.

2.2 Calculate Return

The game ends, producing a final result GGG (for example: win G=1G=1G=1, lose G=−1G=-1G=−1).

2.3 Build Training Dataset

Extract every step taken in this game to form training samples: (St,At,G)(S_t, A_t, G)(St​,At​,G). Note that all steps in this game share the same final outcome GGG as the label.

2.4 Supervised Learning Update

Feed the massively collected samples into the neural network. Calculate the error between the network’s predicted value Q(St,At)Q(S_t, A_t)Q(St​,At​) and the true outcome GGG (typically using Mean Squared Error, MSE). Update the neural network’s weights through backpropagation, making the network’s predictions increasingly closer to the true outcomes.

2.5 Iterative Loop

Use the updated, stronger network to restart from step 1, continuously iterating until the network converges into a top-tier expert.

3. Why Can DMC “Outclass” Traditional Algorithms in Poker?

This is the soul of understanding DMC’s principle. Poker is an imperfect information game with enormous hidden information (opponents’ hole cards).

3.1 Fatal Flaw of Traditional DQN (TD Method): Error Accumulation

In poker, since you cannot see opponents’ cards, your estimate of the “next step value” is often wrong. The TD method uses this erroneous estimate to update the current value, causing errors to accumulate like a snowball. Eventually, the AI becomes blindly confident, overestimating certain actions that appear promising but are actually fatal.

3.2 DMC’s (MC Method) Superiority: Law of Large Numbers Eliminates Variance

Although the outcome of a single MC game is greatly affected by “luck” (card distribution), leading to extremely high variance, it is absolutely unbiased.

DMC’s solution is: Exchange extreme computing power for massive data. When self-play reaches tens of millions or even hundreds of millions of games, according to the Law of Large Numbers, the element of luck is completely smoothed out. The neural network ultimately learns the pure long-term expected win rate, stripped of luck.

4. Three Engineering Pillars That Make DMC Feasible

Pure theoretical Monte Carlo methods converge extremely slowly. The reason DMC has succeeded in modern AI (such as DouZero) is due to three key engineering optimizations:

4.1 Action Embedding

Poker actions are not simple “up/down/left/right,” but rather “play three 4s,” “play a straight.” DMC maps complex card patterns to low-dimensional dense vectors, enabling the neural network to understand that “playing 34567” and “playing 45678” are logically similar, greatly improving generalization ability.

4.2 Action Masking

Before the neural network outputs predictions, a hard-coded rule engine forcibly sets the probability of “illegal actions” (such as playing a single card when the opponent plays a bomb) to negative infinity. This not only ensures the AI never violates rules but also allows the network to focus only on a few legal actions, significantly reducing the learning space.

4.3 Massive Parallelism

To combat MC’s high variance, DMC architectures are typically deployed on hundreds or thousands of CPU cores running self-play simultaneously, generating training data with extremely high throughput, using “brute force” to forcefully suppress noise.

5. Summary: The Philosophy of DMC

If we compare the traditional DQN algorithm to a “chess master who loves to deduce moves and emphasizes logical progression”;

Then Deep Monte-Carlo (DMC) is a “street gambler who relies on intuition gained from countless battles.”

The philosophy of DMC is: In imperfect information games filled with uncertainty and deception, logical deduction of intermediate processes is often unreliable. Instead of abandoning complex reasoning, directly fit the true final outcomes through massive real-game sessions, letting the deep neural network learn. It doesn’t ask you “why this move is good,” it only tells you “historical data proves that playing this way leads to the highest win rate.”

6. Practical Application Prospects

In the “Ding Ge Dan” project, DMC can be applied to the following scenarios:

  • Endgame Deduction: Utilizing DMC’s unbiased nature to precisely evaluate the long-term win rates of various card exchange strategies
  • Agent Training: Generating high-quality training data through self-play to improve decision quality
  • Strategy Optimization: Combining action embedding technology to help AI understand the similarity of complex card patterns

Compared to traditional MAPPO/QMIX algorithms, DMC is more suitable for handling highly uncertain scenarios, while multi-agent collaboration algorithms have advantages in team coordination. The combination of both may produce a more powerful hybrid architecture.

  • DouZero: Mastering Dou Dizhu with Self-Play Deep Reinforcement Learning
  • Monte Carlo Methods in Reinforcement Learning

  • Comparison of Temporal Difference and Monte Carlo Methods in Reinforcement Learning
  • AI Solutions for Imperfect Information Games

item.title: Deep Neural Network (DNN) Principles: From Neurons to 'Intuitive' Decision-Making
item.author: 0make@gmail.com (AZ)
item.description:
Introduction

When we talk about artificial intelligence, “Deep Neural Network” (DNN) is undoubtedly one of the most core technologies. But is its principle really that mysterious?

To summarize in one sentence: A deep neural network is a “super function fitter” composed of layers of simple mathematical formulas nested together. Its sole purpose is to learn from massive amounts of data to find the extremely complex mapping relationship between input (such as a hand of poker cards) and output (such as the win rate of that hand).

To thoroughly explain its principles, we break it down into four core modules: basic units, network structure, learning process (training), and why “depth” is so powerful.

1. Basic Unit: Artificial Neuron

The inspiration for DNN comes from biological brain neurons, but mathematically, it’s just a very simple computational unit. A neuron receives multiple inputs and produces an output through two steps of calculation:

1.1 Linear Weighted Sum

Multiply each input xix_ixi​ by a Weight (wiw_iwi​), then add a Bias (bbb).

Intuitive understanding: The weight www represents the “importance” of this input. For example, in poker, the weight of the feature “having a bomb in hand” is definitely much larger than “having a single 3 in hand.” The bias bbb acts as a “trigger threshold.”

Formula:

z=w1x1+w2x2+...+wnxn+bz = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + ... + w_nx_n + bz=w1​x1​+w2​x2​+...+wn​xn​+b

1.2 Non-linear Activation

Put the sum result zzz into an activation function (such as ReLU, Sigmoid).

Intuitive understanding: If there were only linear summation, no matter how many layers the network stacks, it would ultimately be equivalent to a single layer of linear computation, which is meaningless. The activation function introduces “non-linearity,” allowing neurons to decide “whether to be activated” (for example: only when the total card strength score exceeds a certain threshold, output a strong signal).

Formula:

a=Activation(z)a = \text{Activation}(z)a=Activation(z)

Common activation functions include:

  • ReLU: f(x)=max⁡(0,x)f(x) = \max(0, x)f(x)=max(0,x), simple and efficient, currently the most commonly used activation function
  • Sigmoid: f(x)=11+e−xf(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}f(x)=1+e−x1​, compresses output to between 0-1, suitable for probability output
  • Tanh: f(x)=tanh⁡(x)f(x) = \tanh(x)f(x)=tanh(x), compresses output to between -1 and 1

2. Network Structure: From Shallow to Deep

Connecting hundreds or thousands of such neurons together forms a neural network. It is typically divided into three layers:

2.1 Input Layer

Receives raw data. In poker AI, the input might be a vector encoding:

  • “My hand cards”
  • “Historical plays”
  • “Remaining cards”
  • “Opponent behavior patterns” etc.

2.2 Hidden Layers

This is the source of “depth.” The network can have multiple hidden layers (such as 3 layers, 10 layers, or even hundreds of layers). Each layer’s neurons receive the output from the previous layer, perform weighting and non-linear transformation, and then pass it to the next layer.

2.3 Output Layer

Provides the final result. In the DMC algorithm, the output layer may directly output the “predicted win rate (Q-value)” for each legal action in the current situation.

3. Core Mechanism: How Does the Neural Network “Learn”?

When a neural network is first initialized, the weights www and biases bbb inside are randomly generated. At this point, it’s an “idiot,” and its predictions are pure guesses. Its “learning” process is essentially continuously adjusting these www and bbb to make predictions more accurate. This process consists of three steps:

3.1 Forward Propagation: Make a Prediction

Data enters from the input layer and, like passing through a factory assembly line, undergoes “weighted sum + activation function” calculations layer by layer, finally obtaining a predicted value at the output layer (for example: AI predicts that playing a certain card has a 60% probability of winning).

3.2 Loss Calculation: See How Wrong It Is

Compare the AI’s predicted value with the true label (in DMC, this is the actual win/loss result after completing the game, such as 1 or -1).

Use a Loss Function (such as Mean Squared Error, MSE) to quantify this gap. The larger the gap, the higher the Loss value.

Mean Squared Error Formula:

MSE=1n∑i=1n(yi−y^i)2\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2MSE=n1​i=1∑n​(yi​−y^​i​)2

Where yiy_iyi​ is the true value and y^i\hat{y}_iy^​i​ is the predicted value.

3.3 Backpropagation & Gradient Descent: Blame Assignment and Correction

This is the most core and ingenious algorithm of DNN (supported by the chain rule in calculus).

Backpropagation (BP)

Since the final prediction was wrong, who is responsible? The BP algorithm starts from the output layer and works backwards, precisely calculating the “contribution” (i.e., gradient) of each weight www and bias bbb in the network to the final error.

Gradient Descent (GD)

After knowing the responsibility of each parameter, the algorithm fine-tunes each www and bbb along the direction that “reduces error” (the opposite direction of the gradient).

Intuitive analogy: It’s like descending a mountain blindfolded. You (the error) want to know how to reach the valley bottom (minimum Loss), so you test the surroundings with your feet, find the steepest downward direction (gradient), and take a small step down (Learning Rate). Repeat this process, and eventually you’ll reach the valley bottom (optimal parameters).

Update Formula:

wnew=wold−η⋅∂L∂ww_{new} = w_{old} - \eta \cdot \frac{\partial L}{\partial w}wnew​=wold​−η⋅∂w∂L​

Where η\etaη is the learning rate and ∂L∂w\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}∂w∂L​ is the gradient of the loss function with respect to the weight.

4. Why Is It Called “Deep”? (The Magic of Depth)

Early neural networks had only 1-2 hidden layers (shallow networks), and they could only solve simple problems (such as recognizing handwritten digits). The reason “deep” networks (multi-layer hidden layers) are so powerful is that they possess the ability of Hierarchical Feature Learning.

Taking poker AI as an example, when processing data, deep networks automatically form an “abstraction ladder”:

First Hidden Layer

May only learn to recognize the most basic patterns, such as:

  • “Is there a pair?”
  • “Are there consecutive numbers?”

Second Hidden Layer

Combines features from the first layer to learn to recognize more complex patterns, such as:

  • “This is a straight”
  • “This is a small bomb”

Third Layer and Beyond

Further combines to learn to recognize advanced tactical intentions, such as:

  • “The opponent might be bluffing”
  • “The current situation is suitable for using 4 to exchange cards and intercept”

Key difference: Shallow networks require human engineers to manually design these features (Feature Engineering), while deep networks can “automatically learn” these features directly from raw data.

5. Summary: The Role of DNN in DMC Algorithm

Returning to the poker AI (DMC algorithm) we discussed earlier:

  • Monte Carlo (MC) acts as the “grading teacher,” providing the true final outcome (standard answer GGG) for each situational action through massive simulations.

  • Deep Neural Network (DNN) acts as the “student doing practice problems.” It guesses answers through forward propagation and corrects the connections in its brain (weights www) by comparing with standard answers through backpropagation.

After tens of millions of rounds of “practice” (self-play training), the internal weights of this deep neural network are adjusted to an excellent state. At this point, when you give it a new poker situation (input) in actual combat, it doesn’t need to perform time-consuming Monte Carlo simulations. It only needs to perform a very fast forward propagation to instantly output the action prediction closest to the true win rate based on “intuition.”

This is the “chess sense” or “card sense” that deep neural networks give to AI.

6. Practical Application: DNN Deployment in the “Ding Ge Dan” Project

In the “Ding Ge Dan” AI dual-engine architecture, DNN plays a core role:

6.1 Feature Engineering Reconstruction

For special rules such as “3 cards as bomb, 4 cards as hun,” redesign the feature encoding method of the input layer to ensure the network can understand these unique card pattern logics.

6.2 Action Embedding Optimization

Map complex card patterns (such as “play three 4s with a pair”) to low-dimensional dense vectors, enabling DNN to capture semantic similarities between different card patterns.

6.3 Distributed Training Acceleration

Utilize large-scale parallel computing to simultaneously conduct self-play and data collection on hundreds of CPU cores, significantly shortening the training cycle.

6.4 Inference Speed Optimization

After training is complete, DNN’s forward propagation can be completed in milliseconds, meeting the performance requirements of real-time battles.

  • Comparison of Temporal Difference and Monte Carlo Methods in Reinforcement Learning
  • Guide to Choosing Neural Network Activation Functions

References:

  • Deep Learning by Ian Goodfellow et al.
  • Neural Networks and Deep Learning
